The Lincoln Institution

by Mike Bertram and Heidi Sproat 



Introduction

The Lincoln Institution was a charity created by Mary McHenry Cox which operated from 1866 to 1922. It had 4 phases:

1.	A Civil War orphanage funded by the State of Pennsylvania.

2.	An Indian School funded by the Department of Indian Affairs of the Federal Government.

3.	A privately funded Indian school.

4.	A privately funded orphanage for white Protestant boys. 

Mary McHenry Cox 
Mary McHenry was born in 1827. She received a substantial inheritance through railroad investments. In 1856 she founded the Church Home for orphan boys and helped children living on the streets of Philadelphia, initially from her home. Her organizational talents became obvious when she managed the Restaurant Department at the 1864 Great Central Fair in support of local soldiers. The fair was located in Logan Square, Philadelphia. She then founded the Lincoln Institution in 1866. 

In 1880 she married John Bellangee Cox, a prominent Philadelphia lawyerD733. She was then known as Mrs. John Bellangee Cox using the naming conventions of the time. In 1883 they purchased Ivycroft in Tredyffrin township as their summer home. Her marriage was relatively short as her husband died unexpectedly in 1887. In this document we use the name Mary McHenry Cox for events after her marriage. Mary ran the Lincoln Institution from its creation in 1866 to her death in 1906. 

Phase 1 - A Civil War orphanage

Civil War Orphans

In 1863, in the aftermath of the Battle of Gettysburg, the Pennsylvania Legislature debated how to handle the many Pennsylvanian orphans created by the Civil War. These were not orphans in our present sense of the word. They were children who had lost their fathers in the Civil War. Their mothers were usually still alive but there were very few opportunities for them to earn a living in those days and many of them could not support their children. The Legislature decided to allow privately owned, for-profit orphanages to be established which would be funded by the State and supervised by a State-appointed superintendent. The orphanages were segregated with one school for colored children and the remainder for white childrenSOS1, SOS2.

The schools provided an education for the orphans. Those between 8 or 9 (as an exception the Lincoln Institution took in younger children) and 13 years old were in full time education. At the age of 13 they were sent out for work experience (in the Lincoln Institution’s case with Philadelphia center city firms while other orphanages only provided work experience in agriculture) and the children also attended night classes. The students aged out of the system at 16, but those in the Lincoln Institution were allowed to remain, paying a nominal rent.

The State Superintendent managed the arrival and departure of orphans from the schools, and you often find records for orphans returning home at their mother’s request.

13 orphanages were initially set upSOS1. The orphanages were located in rural areas, the nearest one to the Tredyffrin -Easttown area being at Chester Springs. The first superintendent was Dr. Thomas Burrowes.

The Superintendent then invited Mary McHenry to set up an orphanage for white Episcopalian boys, and the Lincoln Institution was born.

Does this sound as strange to you? Why would the Superintendent go out of his way to set up such a limited intake charitable orphanage and not make a similar offer to other religious groups?

Mary McHenry was not a meek woman who sat around waiting for events to happen. She made things happen.

We can postulate that it happened along these lines. Mary decided she wanted to set up an orphanage (she had previously helped children living on the streets of Philadelphia from her home), so she talked to her friends in the higher echelons of Philadelphia society, and to politicians and Episcopalian church leaders she knew. Then someone important whispered into the Superintendent’s ear that it would be a really good idea if he approached Mary with the offer to fund an orphanage if she would start one.

He did and everyone was happy.

Mary agreed with the Superintendent to take in 100 orphan boys. The first steps were to set up a controlling charity and to obtain accommodation. The Lincoln Institution was born in 1866. Mary McHenry purchased a building on 11th Street in center city Philadelphia for the charity. In 1871 the Educational Home was built, and finally the PoNeMah site was created in 1884.

The Soldiers’ Orphans School, 1863 - 1884

Mary had previously run the Church Home for orphans out of her house in center city Philadelphia. The Lincoln Institution was only for white boys of Episcopalian parents (all the schools were racially segregated. There was a separate school for colored children), there were also non-denominational schools for both boys and girls.

In 1866 at least 78 boys were recruited for the school. After the first year the school usually had over 100 pupils. Originally the orphans were children of soldiers killed in the Civil War. Later the scope was extended to all orphans of soldiers who served in the Civil War. The names and details of over 500 orphans have been collected and can be searched. A property was purchased on Eleventh Street in Philadelphia for the Lincoln Institution. Mary McHenry, showing her amazing ability for collecting donations, managed to collect enough money to cover the total cost of the property. The location of the school is shown on the following mapGPGN:

The Organizational Structure of the Lincoln Institution

The Lincoln Institution was set up in 1865 with a two-level organizational structure with a Board of Council and a Board of Managers. General George Meade, of Gettysburg Fame, chaired the meeting that set up the Institution and served as the first President of the Board of Council until his death in 1872. Many members of the Council were Episcopalian church leaders. The Board of Council was an all-male protective shield that allowed Mary McHenry Cox and her lady colleagues to run the orphanage through the Board of Managers, which was all-femaleD871. 

There were two treasurers, one for each board, and two financial reports were produced each year.

The Lincoln Institution was the only charity school; all the other schools were run as for-profit organizations. The State of Pennsylvania provided funding.

Educational Home

In 1871 Mary Gibson donated over 6 acres of land on 49th Street in Philadelphia to the Lincoln Institution. The details of this transaction are unclear, with differing reports. This land had been part of the original Bartram estate. It was given the name of the Educational Home. At the time of the donation the property was on the edge of the city.

The Educational Home was incorporated as a separate non-profit organization from the Lincoln Institution and the organizational structure was duplicated. The reason for this structure is unclear. This meant there were then four Boards and that four financial reports were produced each year.

The property was split into 4 quadrants. One quadrant was sold or leased to the Philadelphia Traction Company; 2 quadrants had houses built on them, the rents and leases being used to bolster the Educational Home finances. The fourth quadrant was the site of the Educational Home. There was also a dairy farm probably in this quadrant as reported in the annual reports.

For around $40,000 a building was constructed on part of the site and occupied in 1878. The cost of the building was a huge amount for those days but Mary McHenry, with her prowess in eliciting donations, seemed to have no trouble obtaining the necessary funds. A description of the interior of the Educational Home is availableD873, and the following lithograph of the buildingLI3.

After the contraction in the size of the Indian school in 1900, the Educational Home was sold in 1903. The home was torn down and replaced by housing.

Finances & Education

The school provided an education for the boys. Those less than 13 years old were in full time education. At the age of 13 they were sent out for work experience with Philadelphia center city firms and also attended night classes. An amazing number of over 180 local firms participated in this program. At the age of 16 the boys aged out of the orphan’s system, but a number stayed at the Institution while having full time employment.

The funding by the State of Pennsylvania initially was $110 per child per year, later raised to $130. The Lincoln Institution soon realized that this funding was inadequate to cover the costs in center-city Philadelphia. The rural for-profit organizations, however, seemed to be able find it sufficient to operate. The program was altered to make the orphanage more self-sufficient and to structure the donations in order to make them more stable. These changes were adequate during the Soldier’s orphans’ phase of the Institution but became a significant problem during the Indian School phase.

The main features of the self-sufficiency effort were: 

Food production on farms

Baking, mainly bread

Shoe-making and weaving for the orphan’s use

Broom-making for sale

Clothes washing



It was estimated that the actual cost per student was nearer $130 in 1867LI4. The gap was funded through scholarships and donations. There were many other donations, mainly of non-monetary items, such as food, coal, and railroad ticketsLI5. As well as an academic education the boys were also given military instruction, mainly in the form of marching.

ScholarshipsD867

After Mary McHenry’s instigation in 1870 the local Episcopalian churches, such as St. Lukes, James, and Mark funded annual scholarships. General George Meade donated the first endowment. Scholarships were generally $150. Individuals also funded scholarships, some under their own names, some under other titles, for example the West Chester Scholarship was funded by Miss Susan Gorgas, who also funded 3 other scholarships. At the peak there were 46 scholarships in one year, covering nearly half of the orphans at the Institution. Some individuals donated the whole $150 themselves, while others collected smaller donations to add up to $150. The scholarships continued as long as there were soldier’s orphans at the Institution.

Later, the Institution received from the State $150 per year for those children between the ages of 13 and 16. These boys received up to $3 a week for their work at outside organizations which was placed in savings accounts for them. 

Work Experience

Generally, the Pennsylvania Orphan schools had rural locations. This made it almost impossible to give the boys job experience at businesses, so they were employed in agriculture. That situation prevailed until 1895 when a site at Scotland, Franklin County, was set up. The Lincoln Institution, on the other hand, being in center city Philadelphia, was surrounded by a variety of businessesD877. Mary McHenry Cox and her helpers took advantage of their location and placed virtually all the boys over 13 years old with local businessesD874. In several of the annual reports the location of their work is listed. There were 270 employers of Lincoln Institution orphans, in the 1870s and early 1880s, including the employer’s addresses.

From this data we have created a Google Maps applicationmap that shows the distribution of the employers, most of them located EAST of Broad Street. This area is where most of Mary McHenry Cox’s team lived.

Farming

640 acres of land in the Dakotas (now South Dakota) were purchased and in 1880 a group of older orphans travelled from Philadelphia to the Dakotas to set up the Meade farmD872. The farm did not survive for long. 

Additionally, there was a farm including a dairy, likely part of the Educational Home, 49th street site, which is mentioned in the 1884, 1886, and 1887 annual reports.

Farming also took place at the Ponemah site, (which was initially in Wayne, it then moved to Upper Merion and later extended into Tredyffrin) and is noted in the 1885, 1895, and 1910 decade annual reports. 

How the Children were treated (1881)

The Institution had a library with books, games, and magazines. There were also entertainments throughout the yearD876. The issue of discipline among the older boys always seemed to be a problem.

Around 1875 William Hugg was appointed as Superintendent of the School. His wife took the position of matron.

In 1881 complaints were made by some of the children about how they were treated at the School. The Philadelphia Times took on the case and interviewed several of the children at their places of work20. Hugg was man who easily lost his temper and become violent. He assaulted the children and whipped them with knotted ropes and other instruments. Children were also put in chains, placed in solitary confinement in a â€˜dungeonâ€™, fed only bread and water, and with the rats being their only companions.

A committee was set up to review the factsD794, D796, D800. The descriptions by the children and by Hugg were very similar. Hugg said this was how he maintained discipline in the School. Hugg retained the confidence of Mary McHenry Cox and few changes were made. There are no signs that the Church leaders at the head of the Board of Council had a problem with how the school operated. It was acceptable for a boy to be whipped for going to church as he was disobeying ordersD799, D792. There were no resignations from the Board of Council, but a number of church organizations withdrew from providing scholarships. There was a short review of the case in the 1882 Lincoln Institution annual report, which distorted the facts.

The scholarship scheme was renewed and a number of new scholarships were created. Another significant change was made. The Institution no longer accepted any older orphans into the School. This, and the aging out of orphans, caused a reduction of the number of boys in the school from 100 in 1881 to 37 in 1885. This reduction set the foundations for the next stage in the Institutionâ€™s existence, that of an Indian schoolD785.

The End of the State Orphans’ Schools

The state scheme for orphans continued until 1885 when a scandal and corruption at the for-profit schools was uncoveredSOS2. 

The names and other details of over 550 Orphans who were part of the Lincoln Institution have been collected as a spreadsheet and can be searched. Contact the authors if you would like to search this resource. It is planned to make the information available in the form of a searchable database. 

Phase 2 - An Indian School 

The first Government Indian school was organized in 1879 in Carlisle, Pennsylvania by Colonel Richard Henry Pratt, an army officer. Its goal was to destroy Indian culture, identities, languages, and traditions through assimilation and espoused the slogan “Kill the Indian, Save the Man”CAR1. The students had their hair cut short and were given majority-culture apparel to wear. They were assigned Americanized names and the use of Indian names was banned. They were forced to use the English language, being punished if they used their native tongue. Indian rituals were banned, and the students forced to attend Christian services.

The Indian Schools continued to be run using this philosophy until Pratt was removed from his position in 1904. The schools continued after that time but with more Indian input on how they were run was allowed over time. In 2022 the Department of the Interior published a review of the Indian SchoolsLI10.

In 1883 a group of students from the Indian school in Carlisle stayed at the Lincoln Institution for a few days while visiting an exhibition in Philadelphia. By this time most of the orphans from the Civil War were â€˜aging outâ€™ of the Lincoln Institution (and other) schools. To stay in existence the Lincoln Institution would have to take on a different role. The Institution decided to convert to being an Indian school as part of the government assimilation program and contracted with the Federal Government to take 100 Indian girls and, a little later, an additional 100 Indian boys. The Federal Government paid $167 per year for each student26. Some students were transferred from the Carlisle School while others were recruited directly from tribes. Mary McHenry Cox visited the Indian reservations and promoted the Institution, while others were recruited by agents.

Transition

The change from the Soldiers’ Orphan School to the Indian School did not mean that the orphans were moved out of the school, rather that no additional orphans joined the school. The 1893 annual report shows there were still three orphans in the school.

There was publicity of the change. Professional photos were taken of the girls at the Spread Eagle Inn, and of the temporary chapel in Wayne; a reporter was recruited to write an article on the schoolD854 and articles appeared in the local Philadelphia papersD725, D726, D734.

The girls lived at the Lincoln Institution site on 11th street in Philadelphia and at the Ponemah site in the summer, while the boys were accommodated at the Educational Home on 49th street. Some of the boys worked and lived on farms during the growing season.

The Challenges of an Indian School

Providing education of the Indian children was a much more difficult task than for the Soldierâ€™s orphans. The main reasons for this were the following:

The Indians had to first learn English. Some became proficient but others struggled with the language and were likely sent back to the reservations. The girls seemed to be overall better linguists than the boys.



At a minimum some of the culture of the employers would need to be accepted by the Indian boys in order to train for a job.



The financial situation was grim. The government stipend was inadequate and there was little enthusiasm by the public to donate to the Indian cause. No scholarships were set up for the Indians. This was unsurprising since the Indian Wars were recent memories (Custer’s defeat at Little Big Horn and the Sioux Black Hills War both occurred in 1876), and fighting was continuing at a generally lower level (the Wounded Knee Massacre was not until 1890). Geronimo and his group of Apaches did not surrender until 1886LI12. In 1893 and 1896 there were financial panics and resulting depressions may very well have affected the finances.



The equipment for the boy’s job training and the availability of apprenticeships were inadequate. The result was that boys had nothing to do for many months. A recipe for trouble.



The skills taughtD917, for example, the type of farming, were not necessarily related to the state of the reservations the students returned to.



Assimilation as portrayed by Richard Pratt was a one-way process. The Indians only had to accept the white man’s society. In fact, it is a two-way process, the society has also to accept the group that wants to become assimilated. The evidence is that in the late 1800s the major part of Philadelphia society was unwilling to accept Indians (see Luther Standing Bear article as an example). 



Recruitment and Length of Stay

Initially a number of the Indians were transferred from the Carlisle School. In 1890 Mary McHenry Cox visited Indian Reservations to better understand the situation and to recruit; there were agents who recruited others31, and some were sent as representatives of their tribesD798. The standard lengths of stay at the Lincoln Institution was either 3 or 5 yearsD879. Some students left earlier. The reasons for them leaving are unknown. There was also a minority who stayed longer than 5 years. Again, the reasons are unclear but some seemed to be retained as they were star pupils that could be brought out for visitors to show what a good job the Institution was doing.

A similar initiation process was used at the Lincoln Institution as at the Carlisle school. Ah-nen-la-de-ni, aka as Daniel La France, in his autobiographyD729, describes the procedure for the boys. “The first thing that happened to me and to all other freshly caught young redskins when we arrived at the institution was a bath of a particularly disconcerting sort. We were used to baths of the swimming variety for on the reservation we boys spent a good deal of our time in the water, but this first bath at the institution was different. For one thing, it was accompanied by plenty of soap, and for another thing, it was preceded by a haircut that is better described as a crop.

The little newcomer, thus cropped and delivered over to the untender mercies of larger Indian boys of tribes different from his own, who laughingly attacked his bare skin with very hot water and very hard scrubbing brushes, was likely to emerge from the encounter with a clean skin but perturbed mind. When, in addition, he was prevented from expressing his feelings in the only language he knew, what wonder if some rules of the school were broken.

After the astonishing bath the newcomer was freshly clothed from head to foot, while the raiment in which he came from the reservation was burned or buried. Thereafter he was released by the torturers, and could be seen sidling about the corridors like a lonely crab, silent, sulky, immaculately clean and most disconsolate.

After my bath and reclothing and after having had my name taken down in the records I was assigned to a dormitory, and began my regular school life, much to my dissatisfaction. The recording of my name was accompanied by a change which, though it might seem trifling to the teachers, was very important to me. My name among my own people was ‘Ah-nen-la-de-ni,’ which in English means ‘Turning crowd’ or ‘Turns the crowd,’ but my family had had the name ‘La France’ bestowed on them by the French some generations before my birth, and at the institution my Indian name was discarded, and I was informed that I was henceforth to be known as Daniel La France.

It made me feel as if I had lost myself. I had been proud of myself and my possibilities as ‘Turns the crowd,’ for in spite of their civilized surroundings the Indians of our reservation in my time still looked back to the old warlike days when the Mohawks were great people, but Daniel La France was to me a stranger and a nobody with no possibilities. It seemed as if my prospect of a chiefship had vanished. I was very homesick for a long time.”

The process for the girls was similar and is described in a newspaper article where the house mother was interviewedD854:

The Indian girls seem to progress well with some being transferred to the local Philadelphia school where they successfully advanced. A few of the boys were also transferred to a local school. 

Unlike the situation with the Soldiers Orphans, there was difficulty getting employers to accept Indian boys for apprenticeships so not all the older, teenage boys had work to go to. This was a recipe for trouble, but the situation seemed to hold until 1895.

The PoNeMah siteLI13

Mary McHenry Cox decided that the Indian girls needed to move out of the city in the summer to escape the heat and humidity. Mary and John Bellangee Cox had a summer home in Tredyffrin called Ivycroft. The Institution refurbished the nearby colonial era Spread Eagle Inn in nearby Radnor Township for the girls. The Inn accommodated the girls in the summers of 1884 and 1885.

There are many interesting features of this photo. We originally thought that the woman in black on the left-hand side of the balcony might be Mary McHenry Cox, but now we think it is probably Mrs. Sievwright, the House MotherD854. The group of men and boys in the lower right-hand side of the photo are also intriguing. The orphans wore coats with big brass buttons during their marching practice so the boys are likely to be some of the orphans, but we have little idea of why they were at the Spread Eagle. We suspect that the 3 Indian men sitting in the front row could be translators.

The site was named Ponemah, a word used by Longfellow in his poem ‘The Song of Hiawatha’.LI14 Meanwhile Mrs. Cox looked for permanent accommodation as the Inn could not be purchased. Eventually a plot of land was acquired in Upper Merion, very close to the Cox’s summer estate. In 1886 accommodations on the Ponemah site were built and occupied that summer. Later the site was extended into Tredyffrin township.

Finances

The government money of $167 per student was insufficient to provide adequately for the children and, in contrast to the Civil War orphans, it was much more difficult to solicit donations.

In 1886 twenty Indian boys were placed on farms. Unlike some of the other Indian schools, the wages of five dollars a month were kept by the Indians, four dollars were placed in an individual Saving Fund, while the fifth dollar was kept by the boy for spending money. This system seemed to be in place at least until the Institution stopped accepting Federal money.

The Educational Home was focused on self-sufficiency as can be seen from the description of activities from 1893: 

Bread making - 66,337 pounds of bread, 92,245 rolls, 52,620 cakes, 4,978 pies. Some of this bread was sold to the Lincoln Institution bringing in $957.



Clothes washing for the Lincoln Institution brought in $382.



Shoe making and repairing â€“ 403 pairs of shoes made, 777 pairs mended, 12 pairs of boots made (all for internal consumption).



Tailoring â€“ 96 coats made, 80 vests, and 181 pants (again for internal consumption).



In other years there was broom and whisk making and weaving; the brooms being sold externally.



Funding Difficulties

In 1895 the Senate budget proposal did not include money for either the Lincoln Institution or the Hampton School (who were the two schools not part of the Department of Indian Affairs). They were both charged with sectarianism. After a deal of argument, the appropriation was included in the budget. A similar argument occurred in 1896. Then in 1899 the discussion of the budget proposal was disrupted by a complaint against the Institution. Eventually, in 1900, the Institution withdrew its request for funds and downsized.

Training

In 1895, out of 103 boys, 9 boys were learning trades outside the Home: 1 blacksmithing; 1 piano making; 2 Harness Making; 2 carpentering; 2 shoe-making; 1 printing. 20 boys were learning trades in the Home: 7 shoemakers, 6 engineers, 5 bakers, and 2 tailors. 21 boys worked part time on farms. It is unclear what the other 53 were doing.D917

1895 - 1899

The period from 1895 to 1900 was when the financial issues of running the school hit home. Perhaps that was the aftermath of the panics and depressions of 1893 and 1896? There was insufficient money to recruit staff of any experience or expertise. There was also insufficient money to provide decent meals for the boys and their clothes were rags.

Richard Pratt was initially very supportive of Lincoln Institution but, over the years, his position changed, and he was very antagonistic.D731

How the Children were treated (1895) 

Problems surfaced with the appointment of George Jackson as superintendent in November 1895. He was a sadist brute, merciless flogging the boys for the slightest deviance from the rules. A complaint was made to the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children. Jackson was interviewed (together with the matron and teacher, who saw and heard nothing).D883 He used the same excuse for the violence that former Superintendent Hugg had done with the Orphans, that this was the way he kept order in the school. Many testimonials of the treatment doled out by Jackson were collected.D915 Before the investigation was completed Jackson disappeared, taking with him money that the boys had earned at work.

After Jackson there was a continuing, rapid turnover of staff. 

Daniel La France â€“ “The length of the agreement with the recruiter was unclear, normally it was 5 yearsD879 but in some cases it was extended. The reason why I and others like me were kept at the school was that we served as show scholars -- as results of the system and evidences of the good work the Institute was doing. When I first went to the school the superintendent was a clergyman, honest and well meaning, and during the first five years thereafter while he remained in charge the general administration was honest, but when he went away the school entered upon a period of changing administrations and general demoralization. New superintendents succeeded each other at short intervals, and some of them were violent and cruel, while all seemed to us boys more or less dishonest. Boys who had been inmates of the school for eight years were shown to visitors as results of two years' tuition, and shoes and other articles bought in Philadelphia stores were hung up on the walls at public exhibition or concert and exhibited as the work of us boys. I was good for various show purposes. I could sing and play a musical instrument, and I wrote essays which were thought to be very good. The authorities also were fond of displaying me as one who had come to the school a few years before unable to speak a word of English.”

Then in 1898, Daniel and a couple of other children had made a complaint about their treatment to the Indian Rights Association.

How the Children were treated (1898) 

The charges made were: a) uncleanliness in the school; b) insufficient and ill-cooked food; c) lack of proper clothing; d) inefficiency on the part of the Superintendent and occasional undue violence in punishments; e) lack of any real industrial training and of systematic teaching, with consequent undue idleness in the school. This incident has been described by Lena Lannutti in her article entitled “We Have No Tribes”.LI15

The Indian Rights Association investigated the complaint and eventually produced a report which was a devastating critique of the operation of the Boy’s School at the Educational Home.D782 In the end, Mrs. Cox had little choice but to withdraw the request for Government Funds and in 1900 she downsized the Indian School so it could exist using only private donations.

In response to his complaint, Ad-nen-la-de-ni was put in the Institution ‘jail’ (a converted stable) and given only bread and water. Someone sympathetic to his situation left the jail door open which allowed him to escape. He travelled to New York and was accepted into a nursing school, but he lost all the money in his saving fund.

The names and other details of over 900 Indians who were part of the Lincoln Institution have been collected as a spreadsheet and can be searched. Contact the authors if you would like to search this resource. It is planned to make the information available in the form of a searchable database. 

The only photograph of a group of Indian boys from the Institution that has been found is a group of Wichita boys.D943 As well as the 1884 photo of the Indian girls, there is also a photo of a small group of girls by Julius Sache.D120 

Phase 3 - A privately funded Indian school.

Bereft of government money, the Indian School reduced its size, to around a quarter of what it had previously been, so that it could survive financially on the available donations. Many of the Indians were moved to the Indian School in Carlisle.D763 The remaining pupils were mainly girls. As part of the contraction of the Indian School the Educational Home building and site were sold in 1903 leaving the 11th Street and Ponemah sites.

Very little information is available on this period in the Institution’s history as no annual reports have been found, though there are a few newspaper reports.LI16 For example, it is unclear how students were recruited and how much they were allowed to follow their culture. 

Phase 4 - A privately funded orphanage for white Protestant boys.

After Mary McHenry Cox’s death in 1906 the Institution reverted to its original scope - to be an orphanage for white, protestant boys. The Ponemah site continued to be used and some Indians continued to be accommodated as can be seen from the newspaper reports, LI17 and the annual reports from the 1910s.

The annual reports of the Lincoln Institution for the period 1911 to 1919 include several photographs of the orphans, many appearing multiple times. The dates when these photographs were taken are unclear, but probably in the 1910s. Some of the photos were taken at the 11th Street building in PhiladelphiaD788. The following photographs were taken at Ponemah and provide views of the site that are otherwise unavailable. 

Emily Exley 1924 to 1956

The Lincoln Institution merged with the Big Brother organization in 1922. In 1924 the Ponemah site was sold to Emily Exley,D766 who already owned an adjacent property. Over the following decades, Emily sold portions of the property, presumably for housing development. In 1956 she transferred the remainder to a trust to benefit the Boy Scouts Paoli Troop #1, who are located on the site.

Ivycroft

After Mary McHenry Cox’s death the Ivycroft estate became associated with the Jefferson Hospital as is shown in the following atlas extract: 

Information Sources

Information Sources

Annual Reports

Forty-five annual reports for the Lincoln Institution and its later sister organization, the Educational Home, have been found, dating from 1865 to 1917.LI19 The biggest gap in these reports is from 1899 to 1910. The reports have all been digitized and analyzed. It is important to realize that these reports, many of which are from 30 to 40 pages long, are promotional material, and that negative facts are ignored or quickly passed over or sublimated.LI18

The reports typically included: 

A list of the committees and their members

Reports from the Chaplains and Physicians

A Secretary’s report

Financial reports from the Treasurers

A list of students

A list of life members

A list of donations

Work done in the Institution

Produce of the farm(s)

Subscriptions to Scholarships



In 1871 the Educational Home was created as a separate charity from the Lincoln Institution although it was run by the same group of managers. The Home produced its own annual reports. The Educational Home housed the older boys during the Soldiers orphan’s period. During the Indian School period the Home housed the Indian boys, while the 11th Street site housed the girls. Cemeteries and Graves

The Lincoln Institution received a donation of plots at the Woodlands Cemetery. Documents and images related to the Woodlands Cemetery and the Orphans and Indians buried there can be found at D833.

Later Fernwood Cemetery was used for burials. No details on the location of the graves at Fernwood have been found.

An Analysis of Orphan’s Deaths at the Lincoln Institution can be found at D837. An Analysis of Indian Deaths at the Lincoln Institution can be found at D801. The last 2 references also link to the death certificates. 

Also see the article ‘When Death Records Reveal a Whole Lot More’ by Heidi Sprout. 

Lists of Orphans and Indians

A list of the orphans known to have attended the Lincoln Institution can be searched here. A list of the Indians known to have attended the Lincoln Institution can be searched here.

A spreadsheet containing all the information found about orphans at the Lincoln Institution can be found at LI20

A spreadsheet containing all the information found about Indians at the Lincoln Institution can be found at LI21

List of Employers

A categorization of the employers of the orphans in Philadelphia can be found at D877. Testimonials concerning orphans employed by center-city Philadelphia Businesses can be found at D874.

No information has been found on orphans or Indians who were employed on local farms during the summer months.

Location of Indians in 1898

As part of the campaign to retain Federal funding in 1898, a list was created of Indians who had been at the Lincoln Institution together their present location and employment. This information has been added to the spreadsheet of Indians which can be found here. 

Additional Material

Additional material has been found in newspaper reports, and reports from other related organizations, which are available through the Internet. Over 180 documents have been transcribed and loaded onto the Document Database, where they can be read and searched.LI2

Epilogue

The Lincoln Institution was a charity, full of people with good intentions. As a Civil War Orphans’ school, it broke new ground in providing occupational training for careers in a rapidly industrializing society.

As an Indian school it was run with the arrogant belief that the Indian culture had nothing to offer. It did offer an education, especially for the girls, that gave them opportunities to bridge between the old culture and the new. Unfortunately, the boy’s school decayed in the 1890s due to financial and other pressures. There was also an ongoing problem with unfit Superintendents being recruited who used severe physical punishments on the boys. The Lincoln Institution never seemed to devise working procedures for handling teenage boys.

Acknowledgments

Among others, the following provided help on this project: Roger Thorne, Michael Krasulski, Jim Gerencser, Lena Lannutti, and Meg Wiederseim.

References and Notes

See here for a list of all the references and notes.

References and Notes

The reference labels below have been devised especially for this article. They are grouped as follows:

CAR - Carlisle Indian Industrial School

D - documents in the TEHS Document database, the number in the label is the document number in the database

GPGN - Greater Philadelphia GeoHistory Network

LI - Lincoln Institution, followed by a sequential number

MFarm - Meade Farm

MMC - Mary McHenry Cox, followed by a sequential number

SOS - Soldiers’ Orphans School, followed by a sequential number

content:
Luther Standing Bear was a Sioux Indian, and the son of a chief, who had heard of the Indian School being set up in Carlisle. So, he made his way to Carlisle only to find there was nobody there as Richard Pratt, the director, was away trying recruit Indians for the school. He was thereby the first pupil at Carlisle and he became a prized pupil. When the Wanamakers requested 2 Indians to come and work at their store in center-city Philadelphia, he was the first choice.

While he was working at Wanamakers he lived in the Educational Home. There he witnessed the first efforts of Mary McHenry Cox to bring Indian boys to the Lincoln Institution school. At the weekends he would join with the other Indians at the Home in their singing and music-making. 

Luther wanted to stay on at Wanamakers but not to live at the Educational Home. He could not find anyone who was willing to provide board for him in Philadelphia. In the end he returned to Carlisle and then his Reservation, where he started his career, which included being part of Buffalo Bill’s Wild West Show and acting in movies.

content:
Introduction

As you drive west along route 30 from Philadelphia through the many towns of the “Main Line” you will eventually come to Berwyn in Easttown Township. If you look around there is little to remind you of the interesting history of the area, particularly as it relates to early America. In spite of this, the history of Easttown colors the reflections of 300 years and numerous generations as it weaves its way through the many eras of our past.

The purpose of this book is to tell the stories that have always surrounded Easttown, to follow the people who founded it and those who sustainted it as well as the legendary charachters who lived or frequented it over 300 years. It is considered a panoramic and colorful chronicle of Easttown growth and development over the years.

To set the stage for the Tricentennial History of Easttown the book begins with men of vision in England and other countries who were attracted by the promise of land. In the “Colonial Period” we learn how the early Dutch, Swedish and English obtained the land and how it was divided and divided again and passed along generation after generation. Although Easttown is not large it is amazing how often land changed hands and how many people were involved. The heritage and customs of these first settlers is highlighted, how they toiled to raise crops and homes, where roads were built to connect the settlements. The religions and their churches are described, as are their customs of birth, death and everyday life, who could vote and the inns where they voted, where social life centered.

This period of colonization transforms the raw land into farms and settlements and local goverment appears. We learn of the village of Cockletown, which in the future becomes Reeseville and finally Berwyn. We learn about the families who lived there. their properties and the dwellings in which they live. This in turn leads to the “Pre-Revolutionary Period” and the further establishment of the rural economy. Soon the residents of Easttown have a front row seat to military events in the War for Independence and we learn of the politics and the involvement of the people in this conflict. Some of the most decisive and exciting events of the war are detailed. We find the township had its share of hardships and heroes.

Following the war the country’s first pike or toll road pleased travelers and it passed through Easttown. The Philadelphia and Lancaster Turnpike followed much the same route as today’s Route 30 Lancaster Pike. This, in turn, we are told, brought taverns to the area, and as the communities grew, schools and churches. Law, too came to Easttown with a Justice of the Peace in 1800. Then came the railroad that cut through Berwyn and took much traffic from the turnpike and caused the decline of the “Tavern”.

The emergence of the railroad led to the beginning of local industry and, with this, population growth and expansion of educational facilities. Several small streams in the area provided waterpower and as a result textile and other mills were built, including a cigar factory. One o fthe mills was Wateroo Mill, which stands today. It became the first post office in Easttown. Then came steam power and gradually these country factories, so far from the markets and lacking cheap and quick transportation, becam abandoned and before long fell into ruins.

The Civil War soon followed and all its heroes and heartbreaks related to Easttown are chronicled here. A look at the politics of the area tells us how they caused changes in Easttown. Then comes a modest growth in population and some prosperity. Next is the aftermath of the war and the movement north of many former slaves who were no free.

Soon America was 100 years old and during this Centennial period of 1876 to 1885 the name Berwyn comes into being and is recognized by the United States Postal Office. The railroad made improvements , one of which they built the red brick Berwyn Train Station in 1881. Water pipes were laid, a library and private schools started, a general store opened in Berwyn, new homes were built and a real estate office appeared. The Wayne homestead becamea tourist attraction until pilfering became a problem. This was not the only crime that came to Berwyn, there was the “Hammer Hollow Gang”, but the Berwyn Protective Association soon put a stop to that. They even had a “Lancaster Avenue Improvement Association,” Progress abounded and Easttown began again to change.

As it developed it became one of the most popular suburbs on Philadelphia’s “Main Line” ... Just east of Berwyn, there was Devon, still in Easttown. It was created as a summer resort. New, large homes were built as resort hotels for the wealthy of Philadelphia. There were places to vacation and get away from the city. Then there wealthy landowners and horse breeders formed the Devon Horse Show in 1896. They needed a convenient place for their money, so Berwyn National Bank was opened. Young William Fritz took over his father’s lumber, coal, and feed business in 1885 (it’s still in the family at the same location). Easttown was still growing and in 1890 the population had doubled in 10 years. All sorts of social organizations came into being, including the fledgling Berwyn Fire Company. It was a time of many changes, from a sleepy town to a thriving active Main Line community.

The final chapters reveal the coming of the automobile and the many wonderful changes it made in Easttown. It includes new people, new industries, World War I, and the post-war era leading up to the “Great Depression,” even President Roosevelt’s WPA and what that brought to Berwyn. We then journey through the era of World War II, the space age and right up to 2004, introducing new people,as we go, until we have documented most everything.

And now it is time to celebrate Easttown’s 300 year Tricentennial ... a township this book proves is “Old in History ... Young in Spirit!”

Chapter 1: In the Beginning

1681 - 1704

On September 15th, 1681 some Welshmen of means purchased 40,000 or 50,000 acres from William Penn (commonly known as the “Welsh Tract”).

{incorrect, it was not a purchase, it was an agreement that the area could be purchased by Welsh Quakers where they could have their own language and customs. It should also be noted that this was a verbal agreement (as were a lot of Penn’s early land sales)}

It was to have been in land lying contiguous, subject to local government of the Welsh Friends to whom the land was apportioned.

It included Haverford, Merion, Radnor, Tredyffrin, and subsequently the greater part of Newtown, Goshen, and Uwchland townships, for Penn was unable to redeem all of his promises of a separate colony or Welsh “barony.” This caused great dissatisfaction, especially after the division of counties cut the Welsh Quaker settlements in two, and they found themselves in a minority. Politically it probably kept some very able men out of office, but gave the death blow to a clan of citizens perpetuating a dialect, for the Welsh had dwelt for ages in proximity to the Englsh and yet preserved their own peculiar language, a language that was forgotten in America in less than three generations.

Wales was not and never had been a rich country. The people were poor, proud, and found it difficult to forgive a slight upon their dignity, but there are degrees of poverty, for some were not so poor that they were under the necessity of engaging in business, the so-called landed gentry. Yet they held that a man might follow any honorable calling or trade and remain a gentleman.

The prime motive that induced the Welshman to give up the impoverished land was to better his condition economically. Wales, too, was in the midst of religious dissentions and many non-conformists suffered persecution from the Established Church and longed to be free of religious conflicts.

Penn’s terms were liberal, 100 pounds sterling for 5000 acres, subject to a quit rent of one shilling for every 100 acres, payable upon the first day of March, forever; which last clause became a dead letter following the Revolution. Many were content to purchase 500 acres or less, and the more affluent were attended by numerous kinsmen, ostensibly as servants, anxious to partake in Penn’s bounty of 50 acres for each, and his guarantee of religious freedom.

Thus the early Welshmen flocked to the western shore of the Delaware. A sturdy, worthy people, more clannish and old fashioned than the English, Dutch, and Swedes who had proceeded them here, but they were the best in Wales. The women is tall beaver hats and outlandish cloaks, were good wives and mothers. They came to brighten up the waste places in the New World. Their fate, however, was not only to toil from sunrise to sunset, but by candle or fire light at night, and their joy to add the feminine touch to the home, to plant the flower garden in the few moments of leisure, and to initiate the young in the rudiments of book knowledge, often with the Bible as the only text book.

Like all other races, the Welsh brought with them all the prejudice of the old country, and the petty differences of crred continued to separate neighbors. Settlers living convenient to a meeting house not of their own persuasion underwent considerable hardship over the rough roads to the house of their own peculiar denomonation.

Although not included in the Welsh “barony,” Easttown did have 100 acres surveyed to Welsh settlers by its First Purchasers. Easttown originally was entirely in the possessionof three Englsih land speculators. Interestingly, the Easttown Welsh were Church of England men, not Quakers.

William Wood and William Sharlow, the latter a prosperous London merchant, appear to have been the so called “First Purchasers” of part of northern Easttown. James Claypoole, a friend of Penn’s, a member of the Free Society of Traders and the first prothonotary of Philadelphia, received a grant for a block of 1050 acres extending across the southwest part. These men were non-residents of Easttown although it is possible that Claypoole had someone is his employ clear off some ground near the present location of Leopard. Newtown “Street” was laid out north from Newtown to near the Easttown border in 1683.

{See the Easttown deed history here, which contradicts some of the statements in this section.}

The Welsh tract in Easttown made up less than 20% of the total township land. It was bounded on the west by the line of Newtown Street road north to what is today the Tredyffrin line. The eastern boundary passed from the corner of today’s Conestoga and Berwyn Baptist roads south across Lancaster avenue and down the little valley of the branch of Darby creek through the western partof Devon back to the border of Newtown. When in 1691 a deed was made by an heir of William Wood to Howell James for “a tract containing 500 acres on the upper end of Newtown,” a preliminary step had been taken in the history of Easttown.

“East Town” as it was originally written, was so called from its position in the county. Settlement was not rpurred by any outstanding resources, waterways, mineral assets or unusually fertile soil. Locations of early saw mills indicate that some of its terrain was covered with forests.A natural feature influencing the land was the many meandering tributaries of Darby creek.

The date assigned to formation of Easttown is 1704. It is first mentioned on the court records by the appointment of William Thomas as its constable, on December 27, 1704. The resident land owners in 1715 were Edward, Ellis, Owen and Morgan Hugh, Philip and John David, David Davis and John Harris, Hugh Jones, Evan Thomas, Richard Evans, and Thomas Edwards, all from Wales and nearly all Friends or Episcopalians. There were 21 taxable settlers in 1730, 25 in 1740, 39 in 1750, and 51 in 1760.

Tradition informs us that a blockhouse for defense against the Indians was erected on an Indian clearing in the northwest angle of Sugartown and Newtown roads, just south of Berwyn, and that the first religious services, some 15 or 20 years before St. David's Church was built, were held there. This clearing was also used by the early settlers as a burial ground.

The first known settlement on land in Easttown took place between 1703 and 1706 at what became know as Travelgwyn. The exact meaning or significance of the name is obscure, but it can be translated as "white toil or trouble." The most ancient deed to the Travelgwyn estate was in Welsh, which had to be produced and translated before the Ivesters could complete a more recent sale.

This tract is just south of Berwyn, on either side of Waterloo avenue and near the foot of Waters’ Hill, and is described in a lengthy deed dated December 4, 1706. 

The tract contained the original log cabin which has been described as a single-storied structure with double-pitched roof, one window and the door in front and a single window in the rear. It was possibly of two rooms, had a large open fireplace, and was situated east of the present stone farmhouse and near to a spring of water on the old Ivester farm, the cabin being last used as a chicken house. At this period Trav-el-gwyn was mostly in timber, the swamp a covert for woodcock, and the branch of the Darby creek swarmed with speckled trout. It was passed on in the family fifteen years later.

The foregoing owners were closely connected, Edward Hughs being a brother to Philip Davies’ wife and Evan Hughs a nephew of the last and son of Edward Hughs, former owner. Philip Davies evidently built the stone house sometime between 1706 and 1722.

On February 20, 1723, this estate was sold by Evan and Ann Hughes, of Easttown, to Griffith Hughes, clerk of Radnor, for 140 pounds. Here it is called Grove Hall, formerly Travelgwyn. The deed was signed by Evan Hughes and the mark of his wife Ann.

The Rev. Griffith Hughes graduated from Oxford in 1732, and was appointed rector of Radnor and Perkiomen (St. David’s and St. James’ Episcopal Churches), but here we find that he was in Radnor and Easttown at least ten years earlier as a clerk and doubtless a student under Rev. Weyman and Rev. Backhouse at St. David’s.

On August 2, 1735, “being the Eight Year of the reign of King George the second,” Griffith Hugh, Clerk, secured a mortgage loan of 95 pounds, 4 shillings from Mordecai Lewis of New Town. The mortgage land description is the first attempt to set forth the one hundred-acre tract by metes and bounds and the first mention of the old graveyard.

On February 13, 1743, by an indenture “Between Griffith Hughs, late of Easttown but now Rector of St. Lucy’s in the Island of Barbados, and John Hughs of Mirian in the County of Philadelphia, Yeoman, Attorney of the said Griffith Hughs Legally Constituted of the one part and Griffith James of Easttown afforsd, Yeoman, of the other part,” Griffith James came into possession of Grove Hall, or Travelgwyn, for the sum of 120 pounds and here he lived for over twenty years.

There is a tradition that his daughter Hannah in her girlhood planted an acorn in the southeast corner of the yard of that which is now known as the Waters’ place, from which grew the great white oak over two hundred fifty years old when it fell on March 24, 1996.

When Griffith James died he left a will dated August 24, 1764 which transferred the property to his wife Ann.

Ann James died October 27, 1773 leaving daughter Hannah sole heir of Grove Hall. Hannah married Whitehead Wetherby a son of Benjamin Wetherby, who was brother-in-law of Dr. Barnado Van Leer of Marple and one time innkeeper at the old Blue Ball Tavern on the Conestoga road.

There was little excitement or romance in the settlement of Easttown for the Indians were few and peaceable. Early in Colonial times the native families were settled upon small reservations: the Okehockings on about 500 acres in lower Willistown along the Ridley creek, another along the Brandywine; reservations that were respected but a little while by the white man. Indeed the Indian left so slight an impression upon our township that not a single native geographical name is in use today.

Both Penn and the early colonists have left some account of the so-called “Indian clearings” and the mulberry and peach trees growing thereon. However, not all are satisfied that these orchards originated with the Indians. While the red mulberry is a native of America, the peach is said to have been indigenous in Persia. It is possible that these orchards were planted with seed brought over by some of the earlier Swedish or Dutch fur traders.

While there was little need of fighting men in the early settlements, there was a great demand for able-bodied men skilled in swinging the ax and in clearing the ground. Penn recommended clearing 15 acres the first year and building a log house 18 x 30 feet, with a partition through the middle and another to divide one end in two smaller rooms, and with a loft over all with a floor of clapboards, and the ground floor of earth.

The forest, mostly deciduous, with more or less pine on the hills, was a century or more old. As it had been long the custom of the Indians to fire the fallen leaves and brush to facilitate the hunting of game, it was usually free of undergrowth and open enough to drive a horse and a light cart in many places.

The Old Lancaster (Conestoga) road, or the King’s highway as it was officially known, followed more or less faithfully an old Indian trail to the mouth of the Schuylkill, for the natives in traversing the backbone of the watershed between the Schuylkill and Delaware, followed the ridge, the path of least resistance. It was the first road, and is said to have been surveyed in 1700 from Philadelphia to the Susquehanna near the mouth of the Conestoga creek, though it was not completed until 1741.

The Provincial Council took the necessary action May 27, 1718, to lay out a road from the Brandywine to the Conestoga. On November 23, 1721, relative to dispute in parallel roads: “It is Ordered that the Road now and heretofore used leading from Philadelphia to Conestogoe, through the Townships of Meirion and Radnor, and laid out by the authority of this Government as far as Thomas Moore’s Mill (Downingtown) on the Brandy Wine River or Creek, be deemed the King’s Highway and public Road.”

They spelled road in those days with a capital “R”, but apparently the exact lines were still a matter of doubt or dispute, since on October 4, 1733, the commissioners appointed January 29, 1730/31 to lay out the road to Lancaster made report that they found it inadvisable to discover where it had been altered while the corn crop was growing, and it continued in an unsettled state until July 20, 1741, when a survey over the entire route was submitted and approved by Council.

It included the more than four miles through Tredyffrin and 292 feet in “East Town”, from the Willistown line to the upper line of Radnor, with 23 angles, and mentions the “Sign of the Ball,” or Blue Ball tavern.

Gulf road was a line of communication as early as 1690, though not officially laid out until 1748, and the Swedesford, in the valley, and the Darby, Newtown, and Sugartown roads were in place in 1700 substantially as today.
