content:
Chapter 2: Colonial Period

1705 - 1760

The rich limestone land of the nearby Great valley was greatly esteemed for agriculture from the start, and the settler thought himself fortunate enough indeed if his allotment fell short of a slice of the North or South Valley hills, which were considered worse than waste ground, the lurking places of the destructive “varmints,” yet, about 1700 certain Welshmen came into possession of land lying contiguous to the old Indian trail, later known variously as the King’s, Great, Provincial, Lancaster or Conestoga road, on the South Valley hills, as wood lots.

Nearly all of the early settlers, except the Germans, were wasteful of the timber. Grand old forests of oak, ash, walnut, maple, birch, hickory, chestnut, pine, cedar, hemlock etc., were felled and rolled in huge piles to be burned to clear the ground. A fine red walnut found near the banks of the Schuylkill was soon gone from this region after it became popular for Colonial furniture.

Doubtless many of the original dwellings were of logs, but as the Welsh were accustomed to stone houses in the old country and had many clever stone masons, thye lost little time in building permanently of limestone. Few examples of log houses exist today. The more or less temporary log hut had large flat stones for corner foundations, stick chimneys daubed with clay, beaten earth floors, moss and clay chinked-log sides, and thatched or split slab roofs.

Few tools were necessary in the construction of a primitive log hut, an accomplished woodsman could build it with no other tool but an ax. The logs were pushed up into place by means of stout pole skids until the walls were about six feet high, when door and window openings were made usually with a crosscut saw and the walls continued upward to the desired height. The door latch and hinges were ingeniously fashioned of wood, and in place of glass there were fastened to the windows the oiled hides of some thin skinned wild animal from which the fur has been removed. The windows were both small and few for the settler, so constrantly in the open, liked to feel the difference when he entered the house.

The Welsh were liberal providers. Before attempting work of any moment, great quantities of eatables and a liberal supply of alcoholic drinks were provided. Some few also learned to provide a hot weather drink compounded of vinegar, ginger and sweetened water, but no harvest seemed complete without strong drink in abundance and it was thought that no foundatiom could be laid, stone wall built, or barn timbers raised without the asistance of alcohol.

The masons constructed their scaffolds of heavy poles fresh from the woods and the put logs were bound to the scaffold poles by hickory withes, no nails being used. For a permanent building the shingles were if possible of pin oak, the kind that split in thin slabs sometimes four feet long, overlapped both ways and fastened with wooden pegs.

The floor was of wide mill-sawn oak plank, ripsawed edges to key, plowed and wedged with loose tongue sometimes when an extra tight floor was desired, and fastened by square pegs in round holes. All of this was done by hand. The plastering was generally done right on the bare stone wall, with the joists and floor boards of ceiling exposed. The partitions were made of wide boards, doubled with wide and overlapped joints, and the whole whitewashed every spring.

When lath were used they were of split oak. Mouldings were planed out by hand and when a carpenter arrived he brought a wagon load of tools and prepared to stay some time. The nails, hinges, locks and other hardware, if not duplicated in wood, were hand wrought by the local blacksmith.

For weeks or perhaps for months before a barn raising, the carpenter and his assistants cut, squared, mortised and bored the heavy timbers, until every piece was ready to hoist in place and the wooden pins driven home -	the work of the assembled neighborhood. A cedar bush lashed to the ridgepole, a relic of still earlier times when a bush on a cottage gable was the sign of ale brew sold within, reminded the owner that a treat was due, and if tradition may be relied upon, the old settlers were no less formidable as trenchermen and drinkers than at heavy labor. An old saw intimates that the Welsh were racially opposed to hard “bone” labor of any kind if a living might be obtained without, but the original colonists of this section were good honest workmen, skilled led in husbandry or craftsmenship and inured to hard labor. A settler might be forgiven almost any sin but the crime of laziness, which was a mortal offense to the whole colony.

Probably the Scotch-Irish pioneer of the hills found the local stone more difficult to quarry or more refractory to use, or perhaps they found the log house more satisfactory. At any rate many of them built substantially of oaken logs, squared and notched, chinked with a mixture of lime mortar and chopped straw. Such buildings had cellars with stout stone walls, and large stone chimneys, with floors and roofs of split oak, pine or cedar. It was the custom, whenever possible, to select the southern exposure of a hillslope, face the sun and bury the rear first story wall below frost level. Many of these buildings have endured for two hundred years and were accounted warmer than stone buildings in the winter.

The recla1mation of the virgin soil required almost super-human effort under a sun many degrees warmer than that to which the Welsh pioneer had been accustomed, and it is said that many of the more mature laborers succumbed soon after the turning of the soil. The young buried their elders in places long since forgotten and busied with the lush crops and the endless distractions incident to frontier life, recorded little of passing events. 

Mowers and reapers for a long time encased their lower extremities in rags as a protection against the rattlers, copperheads and the greatly dreaded “wamper” or “horned” snake (the fabulous “hoop” snake of our grand-daddies) and many believed that this reptile could put its tail in its mouth and roll about like an animated hoop.

We have no records of the dates of the extermination of the various wild animals. However, the “catamounts” (panthers or bobcats) were traced to their dens at Diamond rock, Prissy’s hollow, Mount Misery, the rocks below Leopard and other forgotten harbors and killed with the timber wolves and other stock destroying animals, the scalps of which early commanded a bounty.

The black bear and Virginia deer endured in the hill forests until some time after the beginning of the 19th century, for the Welsh were too busy to become great hunters. A great hollow chestnut tree nearly opposite the old “Black Swan” distillery below Neilley’s log cabin (north side of Old State road, almost within sight of Tredyffrin/Easttown Middle School) was the site of the killing of the last bear found in this vicinity; and an old chronicle states that about 1800, during a mild spell in midwinter, the deer came out of the North Valley hills to feed in the valley. (The deer now come out of Valley Forge Park.) Our National bird, the bald eagle, had its eyrie near Mount Joy until about 1845.

The extermination of carnivorous animals disturbed the balance of Nature and the crow, blackbird, squirrel, and other animals became so numerous as to become a nuisance, and it was found necessary to offer bounties for their scalps. In the aggregate a great sum was paid out for their suppression in Colonial times. As early as 1700 a bounty of three pence a dozen was paid for blackbirds and a like sum per head for crows. In 1749, Kalm, the Swedish traveler, stated that 64,000 black and gray squirrels were killed in the Province on a bounty of three pence each.

The Welsh, though less superstitious than the average emigrant, had a firm belief in the supernatural. Many planted, harvested, butchered, built fences, etc., according to the signs of the moon. They believed that to set out on a journey or begin any new work on Friday would bring bad luck. Quasi-religious belief in miraculous intervention of the Deity, in ghosts and supernatural warning of impending disaster, and that sudden death might outstrip the will of God, were not uncommon.

Perhaps some Welsh farmers believed that if Candlemas day was fair, one could look for six weeks more of winter; yet the quaint rhymester libeled him outrageously when he made him say that he:

Would rather see his wife on her bier
Than a fair second of Februeer.

They had plenty of horses and hogs, but the largest farms seldom kept many cows or sheep, for the reason that there was no local market for fresh meat or dairy products. Wheat was the staple or money crop; rye, flax, potatoes and hay were grown chiefly for home consumption. There was no apology for rye bread but there might be for pie when it appeared:

Here is a dried apple pie, it’s crust is made of rye;
It’s pretty tough, I hope it will be enough.

Although the soil and climatic conditions were best adapted to the Indian maise or corn, very little was raised at first since the settlers had not learned to esteem it. Still it gradually came into favor after they learned from the Indians that seed corn should be planted “when the oak leaf is as big as a squirrel’s ear,” or about the middle of May. The first grist mill in Tredyffrin was built along the Valley creek by Thomas Jarman in 1710; the same year Wm. Davie owned another on the Darby creek a mile below the Easttown border; Nathaniel Grubb had another (late Worrilow’s mill) on Crum creek. Therefore, the local farmer had less than a day’s journey to haul his grain.

The sugar maple does not seem to have been abundant here and the wild honey bee was unknown in America until brought over by the white settlers; “the Whiteman’s flies” as the Indians called them. Cane sugar, molasses and rum were early imported from the West Indies to Philadelphia.

A backwoods settlement is scarcely the place for all the refinements of civilization. There were crude customs and the people were habituated to many things that would now be considered real hardship. Many of the farmers attended meeting in homespun and cowhide boots. The younger generation went barefoot until well into cold weather; the soles of their feet in some instances became so hard and horny that they could crack open a chestnut burr with the bare heel, and, indeed, they felt very uncomfortable when obliged to encase their feet in leather.

In the “good old times” underclothing was not known; abundance of hard work and plain food took its place. Bathing was seldom indulged in during the winter season; an outdoor life made this less imperative and, even during the warmest weather, it was held to be very weakening to the system and opened the pores to disease, to wash too frequently.

The year 1741 is recorded to have had an exceptionally severe winter, deep snows; many cattle and deer perished for want of forage. Colds were frequent and the patient dosed with home remedies. An epidemic during the fall of 1748 is said to have carried off many people, as the doctors were entirely helpless. It had all the symptoms ol pleurisy and usually carried off the victim in two or three days. In 1764 there was an epidemic of smallpox.

Crops were abundant in 1751-52, but the years 1753-55 are said to have been a season of want in the country at large, probably because of the Indian ravages all along the western border.

The use of alcoholic drink was universal. Wine, gin, rum, whiskey, were found in almost every house as specific for fatigue, exposure, snake bite and “chills and ague.” Soon, however, its increased use and abuse moved the elders of the Society of Friends to caution the members against permitting excessive drinking in their houses, especially at funerals and that they should have a care in supplying their friends “more than was good for them.” Soon certain medicinal herbs, native and introduced, made into tea by the good old Quaker mothers, were thought to have all the beneficial and none of the harmful properties of alcohol.

Of play there was little, unless log rolling, house and barn raising, “varmint” hunting, etc., could be so-called, as they were sometimes the occasion for the gathering of neighbors.

An old Welsh game called “Duck on Davy” is played now and then to this day. The “Davy” is a large flat stone and each player provides himself with a small round stone of a pound or so weight and stands back of an imaginary line some ten paces from the “Davy.” The player who is “it”, places his “Duck” on the “Davy” and the other players try to knock it off. If a player misses, he cannot touch his “duck” without danger of being tagged and made “it”, until someone knocks the “Duck” from the “Davy,” when all may grab up their small boulders and run for the line while the player is replacing it. It is a game of quick throwing, running and dodging, and can be rough, especially when someone is hit on the head while bending over his “Duck.” 

Doubtless there were many “bedtime” tales and legends of Wales told at the fireside, but few are preserved. Ghost stories were accepted with great credulity and terror. We are all familiar with the old Welsh-American nursery jingle:

Taffy was a Welshman, 'Taffy was a thief!
Taffy came to my house and stole a piece of Beef;
I went to Taffy’s house and Taffy was not home
Taffy came to my house and sto{e a marrow bone;
I went to Taffy’s house and Taffy was in Bed,
I picked up the marrow bone and threw it at his head.

The early Welsh members of the Society of Friends, settled in the eastern part of Easttown and southeastern redyffrin, attended the Radnor Meeting, Radnortown (now !than), held at the homes of John Jerman, a noted Quaker preacher, and John Evans as early as 1686, although the meetinghouse was not erected until 1693. This was the oldest religious organization in the vicinity and in its more prosperous days it was largely attended from all the country around. The older part of the present building was erected in 1718, but now all records of a long and profitable existence are deposited in the vaults of the Hicksite Friends library, 16th and Race Streets, Philadelphia In 1882, Radnor Meeting fell into disrepair and disuse for nearly fifty years.

There were at later dates, prosperous meetinghouses at Newtown Square, 1696, Goshen, 1722, and East Whiteland, 1726 or earlier; all of which were conveniently near the borders of Easttown.

The Old Welsh Church of St. David’s, Radnor, had its beginnings when the adherents of the Church of England, living at what was then the very edge of the Welsh settlement, came together to worship as they had done at home. The Rev. Evan Evans, rector of Christ Church, Philadelphia, is said to have preached at Radnor every other week from about 1700 until 1718, except for two short absences to return to London. He, too, was a Welshman, a missionary sent out by the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel in Foreign Parts. The events leading to the location of this congregation of Church of England faithful at Radnor Church have not been documented. Only tradition informs us of meetings in a log cabin near Darby creek, in the vicinity of Signal Hill, Easttown, and a short distance from a nearby burial ground. The meeting place then burned.

Tradition continues that some time later a church site was selected to the southeast where the Radnor, Newtown and Easttown boundaries join. It is said that Easttown and Newtown then had more parishioners and that Radnor had very few. A church building was erected there in 1715 during the short period when Rev. John Clubb, another Welshman, was missionary pastor. The oldest gravestone in the burying ground is that of Edward Hughes (1716). 

In the construction of this historic building at St. David’s, it is regrettable that no authentic record has been kept of the personnel and methods of the doubtless skilled volunteer workmen, or the name of the master mason, but the result was that of modest architectural beauty, which leads one to suspect it to be a replica of a church building nestling in some vale in Wales, the home of the Welsh master mason.

The Rev. William Currie, 1737-1775, 1784--1785; was a Scotchman and the last missionary, as the early rectors were called; also the first to preach regularly in English. He was obliged to divide his services between St. David’s, Radnor, St. James’, Perkiomen, and St. Peter’s, East Whiteland. He founded his farm on the southern slope of the North Valley hills in Tredyffrin above the Valley Forge, convenient to all his parishes, convenience at that period being only a relative term. He was situated in the parish of St. Peter’s, about five miles from St. David’s and more than a mile from the Fatland ford which he was obliged to travel on his way to St. James’.

The passing of the Welsh rectors marked the passing of the original Cymric stock and the increase of the English, Scotch, Scotch-Irish, German, Dutch and Swedish emigrants. The English people had felt the competition of the English and Scotch Protestant farmers and manufacturers transplanted in Ireland and the Parliament had closed the home markets to them by arbitrary acts. The result was ruinous to the Irish Protestants and marked the beginning of the ancient grudge that lead to the loss of America to the British crown, for the hegira to the colonies continued until Ireland was drained of most of its enterprising citizens, whose descendants filled the ranks of the Continental army.

During all this period the successive rectors were dependent in a manner upon the bounty of the London society for their small incomes, while the Independent churches had to be self supporting. There seems to have been a day school conducted by Rowland Jones somewhere in the vicinity of St. David’s church sometime between 1720 and 1730. It is clearly established that a school house was built upon the church grounds about 1749, perhaps the successor to an older one, and it endured until 1844.

Keith, holding that members of the Society of Friends could not consistently participate in the administration of the government because of their views, was disowned and later became an Episcopal missionary. In 1717, Thomas Thomas conveyed a small plot on the “Newtown street” as a burial place for the members.

As a commentary upon the supposed intolerance of sects of this period, consider two instances of mixed marriages where husband and wife continued as members of their own peculiar faith without more than personal inconvenience. Two of old Anthony Wayne’s sons, Humphrey and Isaac, were married to women who were Seventh Day Baptists.

A daughter (died 1738, 14th year) and a son (died 1752, 4th year) of Humphrey and Priscilla Wayne; also four children and Elizabeth, wife of Isaac Wayne, are buried here. Both Humphrey (the carpenter) and Isaac (the tanner) were members of St. David’s Episcopal Church. 

Some of the Easttown settlers affiliated with another early Welsh church organization situated near Wyola, Newtown township, known as Seventh Day Baptists (also Baptist Quakers or Keithians). They appear to have been former members of the Society of Friends who had come under the influence of George Keith, a contentious Scotch Quaker holding extreme views regarding the doctrine of non-resistance, and his disciple Abel Noble. 

Elizabeth Wayne, daughter of Richard and Margaret Iddings, died May, 1793, aged 84 years. The inscription on her gravestone reads, “She was a woman of distinguished piety and benevolence.” She was also the mother of Anthony Wayne of Revolutionary and Indian war fame. Some distance below St. David’s church, the site of the house in which Elizabeth Wayne, was born is still pointed out, also the pool in Darby creek on the Radnor line where she was baptized.

Tradition describes Elizabeth Wayne as small in personal appearance but exceedingly competent, as indeed she must have been to manage a household and large estate in the new settlement while her husband drilled the local militia during the French and Indian wars. “Mad Anthony” Wayne, her son, was of course, half Welsh, a fact his biographers have, for the most part, ignored, and his mother, whose religious convictions were wholly against war, lived to see her son the foremost warrior of America.

For a period of one hundred and fifty years the nearest meetinghouse for Easttown Baptists, most of whom were Welsh, was the Baptist Church in the Great Valley. Its history in many respects is peculiarly interwoven with that of our township, as well as with that of the denomination in Delaware and Pennsylvania. 

The church was organized in 1711, and in 1722 erected a meetinghouse of logs, 28 feet square, situated on what we today call Devon State road. The Rev. Hugh David, a Welshman, was the first minister 1711 - 1753. 

Great Valley Presbyterian Church, while inconveniently situated three miles up the valley on the Swedesford road, merits more than a passing notice, since it has many more communicants and contniues to be the burial ground of those of the Presbyterian faith of our community. The congregation, mainly Welsh, assembled as early as 1710 and regularly organized on October 10, 1714 with the Rev. Malachi Jones as minister 1714 - 1720. During the incumbancy of the Rev. David Evans, in 1720, the first building was erected.

In oder to vote in 1739, electors were required to own at least 50 acres, with 12 acres cleared and improved, or 50 pounds in money. Easttown was included in the Crum Creek district with Radnor, Newtown, Upper and Lower Providence. Isaac Wayne, son of the immigrant and father of General Anthony Wayne, repeatedly represented his district in the Provincial Assembly.

John Rees was a lieutenant and Benjamin Weatherby sr. was an ensign in the local company of “Associators” formed about 1748 for protection against the French and Indians. Isaac Wayne is also mentioned as bearing a distinguished part as captain of a local company in the provincial service after Braddock’s defeat, and Cromwell Pearce was a lieutenant in a battalion of foot.

It is probable that the Blue Ball tavern (now Daylesford still standing as a residence near Jimmy Duffy’s) was their headquarters and rendezvous, where they fought their battles over again in front of the bar, traidition of which led historian Dr. Sachse to surmise that it was the mustering place of part of Braddock’s ill-fated expedition of 1755 and the more fortunate Forbes army.

Some of the British soldiers under Dunbar may have stopped there in their long and cowardly retreat to Philadelphia after Braddock’s defeat, but the general opinion is that they are running yet.

Easttown farmers were compelled to furnish some heavy farm wagons for the campaign. According to Government specifications, they were to be furnished with tar and grease pots, drag chains, ax, spade, grasscutter etc., well as extra harness, horse shoes, nails, four horses and an able bodied driver to haul army baggage into the Indian country beyond the Alleghanies. The recompense, however, was not attractive in view of the risk of scalp and property. Even Captain Wayne’s team had to be pressed into service and it never returned.

The taverns along the old Lancaster road (today Conestoga road) catered mostly to the transient trade. The better known in this vicinity were the Fox in Easttown, and the Drove, Blue Ball, Black Bear, and General Paoli in Tredyffrin. The old time inn of the better class was the home of good fellowship and true democracy, managed by an inn keeper of wide acquainttanceship, broad sympathy for his fellow men and giving him the best of home comforts at a moderate compensation. The host welcomed the stranger at his door personally conducted him to his room, introduced him to his fellow travelers and was ever solicitous of his comfort, in short, made him his intimate and life-long friend.

The Blue Ball tavern is said to have been a popular house in early times and was sometimes called the “Half-way House” because it was equidistant from the Schuylkill and the Brandywine by way of the old Lancaster road. Abandoned as a road house when the Lancaster turnpike was built, in 1863 Robert Glenn demolished all but the rear wing and rebuilt it for a farm house.

Easttown’s local tavern was at the sign of the Leopard on the Darby road. It is said to have been built by Adam Roads in 1716. Little is known of its early history beyond the fact that Samuel Wetherby, 1768; Whitehead Wetherby, 1769; Caleb Parry, about 1770-1774; Elisha Worrell, during the Revolution; probably followed by George Steible or Joseph Morgan operated as “ye tavern keeper.” The red frame house, long demolished, at Sharp’s corner on the southeast angle of Sugartown and Leopard roads, was also a tavern at some period. .

The Black Bear (Bull’s Head at one time) at the southwest corner of the Lancaster and Bear roads, was a famous Colonial tavern midway between the Blue Ball and the Paoli. The locality still retains the name of “the Bear,” but unfortunately its history has not been preserved. The building was pulled down by Hugh Steen in 1877.

The Paoli inn appears to have been built by Joshua Evans, the carpenter and the proprietor, 1769-1814, and it is said to have been run by the Davis family for some years, later by the owner with some intervals: Thomas Search, 1779-1780, and Richard Robinson certainly kept it in 1781 and 1797, doubtless many more years.

According to the ingenious tax collector, Easttown landowners in 1753, were Chas. Calling, Nathaniel Claypole (Claypoole), Thos. Crass, Jennie Davis, Ann and Humphrey Ellis, Peter Eliot, Thos. Hingham, Elizabeth Howe!, Benj. and Isaac Hugh, Griffith James, David, Nicholas, and Thomas John; Benj. Junkin, Richard McCadden, Thos. McCain (McKean), John McCorkle, Patrick McCarty, Andrew Meguier (McGuire), John Marran, Morris Matson, Isaac Minshall, Mark Morris, 

Elick-sander (Alexander) Nuckle, Hugh Reed, John Steel, Adam Trehorn, Francis, Humphrey, and Isaac Wayn (Wayne); Hugh Win (Wynne), Edw. William, and Isaac Worrell.

It will be noted that the exclusively Welsh settlements soon exhibited a strong tinge of Scotch-Irish. During the reign of Charles II, the British Parliament placed an embargo upon Irish cattle; the people then turned their attention to sheep, but the English soon felt the competition in wool and woolen goods and closed their markets to them. Many Scotch-Irish Protestants were than reduced to want and the steady emigration to America in 1700 became a succession of waves from about 1717 to just before the Revolution, when there were difficulties in renewing leases in Ireland.

The Scotch-Irish often came with little or no money, but they had a hunger for land, and the Quaker government shrewdly shoved as many as possible out upon the ever- moving frontier, as a living wall between the Indians and the peaceful settlements. As they came on each settlement retained a share, until their number was legion. They proved natural frontiersmen, nor did they stop until the entire West was conquered and there was no longer a frontier to defend. There were also some of their kinsmen, the Scotch. Doubtless numbers were sold into servitude for a specified time, usually four or more years, to pay for their passage according to agreement with shipping masters. It was no disgrace to have been a redemptioner. One had to pay his passage at all events and it was far easier to earn the money in the New than the Old World. Servants were regarded as property and taxed as such. Masters had the right to punish them and the system was capable of great abuse. “White Christian slavery” ceased in 1785.

Thomas Jarman, miller, of upper Tredyffrin, went to town to buy a sleigh about 1715, just when a shipload of redemptioners came in. He bought James Anderson, a bright Scotch boy. Later this boy married Jarman’s daughter, Elizabeth, and ran away to the “wilds of Charlestown.” Still later the parents received a visit from their daughter, bringing her boy Patrick, born in 1719, who later became a captain in the Continental line and a man of property and influence in Charlestown.

There was another and much smaller group forced out of the southern part of Ireland. They depended almost entirely upon farming and grazing, while North Ireland was largely industrial, i.e., manufacturers. This group were originally from the north of England, Episcopalian, and some of them fought with William of Orange in the battle of the Boyne. The Burns’, Hill’s, Hunter’s, Pearce’s,Penrose’s, and Wayne’s were of this class and arrived in this vicinity between 1717 and 1737, feeling that England had not played fair with them in Wicklow, Ireland, but nevertheless associating in the settlements with the English emigrants of Episcopal and Quaker pretentions.

The Welsh came seeking a homeland and the promise of advancement in Penn’s new land. Their hopes of a Welsh “barony” were foreclosed, perhaps, but advance they did. They were joined by the English, emigres from Ireland, and others who labored beside them, but it was a large, beautiful country with much yet to be done.

content:
Chapter 3: Pre-Revolutionary Period

1761 - 1774

The clearing of the wilderness proved too great a task for the Welsh unaided. Great tracts in this community remained untouched. Many of the younger generation sought less strenuous labor. In comparison with the Scotch-Irish, the ideal pioneers of America, the Welsh were more clever and as stubborn in argument as the former were in a fight; but neither the average Welshman nor the typical North of Ireland man were born farmers.

Many of the Welsh were land poor, since the French and Indian wars had increased the taxes and at the same time encouraged the German emigrants and redemptioners to settle throughout the area, from about 1763 to the beginning of the Revolution. The German invasion of this region, like that of the Scotch-Irish, apparently had its inception more on economic than religious grounds.

Many of these tracts lay some distance from the public roads, hence lane or land rights, also water rights, were freely granted. The movement resulted in two or three practically continuous German settlements in the eastern, central, and western parts of the territory extending substantially across the cultivated land. 

That the Germans settled in such numbers as to seriously dispute with the Welsh the language of the community is a matter of doubt. The dream of a Welsh barony had dissipated long since and the Cymric dialect, present only in the earlier records of the religious bodies, had died with the second generation. All legal documents, gravestones, etc., were in English. The English and Scotch spoke no other than English; the Welsh after the first generation understood it, and the Germans had to learn it.

Jacob Frick, of Swiss origin, arrived in America according to the family records in September of 1733 and settled first near Pottstown. About 1740 he married Elizabeth Urner who died in 1757 shortly after the birth of their youngest son, John. It is believed that the Frick family attended Coventry German Baptist Brethren Church. John was reared by Catharine (previous surname unknown) Frick, who was Jacob's second wife.

In 1769, when John was 12 years old, the family moved to a 100-acre farm located in the Chester valley of Tredyffrin township “two miles from Valley Forge,” where they lived during the Revolution, “near the scene of the Paoli massacre, and where the British and Hessian army encamped after the battle of Brandywine.” John was assigned to the Tredyffrin militia, but, as a German Baptist, he did not attend meetings and was fined. Jacob Frick does not appear on the tax list of 1771, but he is listed for 100 acres, two horses, and two cows in 1774 and in subsequent years. The place was located at what a century later was the Abraham farm at New Centerville. John Frick reported a loss of £120 due to depradations during the British encampment in 1777.

The farm “descended” to Nathaniel and Christiana Frick Jones. Christiana was John’s half-sister, as she was the first child of Jacob Frick’s second marriage. The Jones farm was located adjacent to the Frick farm.

The early tax collectors. often illiterate, seldom recorded the occupations of the taxpayers until about a decade prior to the Revolution. Then it appeared that not only nearly all the German emigrants had some trade or another, but that there was quite a sprinkling of the second or third generation of the original settlers with occupations other than that of farmer or farm laborer. However, all or nearly all, including the preachers managed farms of greater or lesser extent. 

John Davis and, later, James Currie, of Tredyffrin, are recorded as physicians; Sampson Davis kept the store at Spread Eagle in 1766 and he was followed by Richard Miles. Christian Workizer had a shop near Howell’s tavern, and Samuel Davis had a store near by, probably at Paoli.

Isaac and Anthony Wayne operated a tanyard at their farm “Waynesborough” and doubtless supplied oak and hemlock tanned cowhide to the cordwainers, or shoemakers, of the vicinity - Amos Jones, John Briggs, Daniel James, John Keck and Boston Rink. The latter took care of the custom of “Cockletown.” Morris Morris, Thomas Jones, and Thomas Williams looked after the footwear and probably the saddles and harness of Easttown.

Benjamin Robinson, followed by Mathias Woolman, were weavers of this period, soon reinforced by James Nealy (Cockletown), John Baker, Henry Ruth, Peter Stickler, Peter Stedler (Spread Eagle), Daniel and Felty Shewalter, with Christian Brannaman (“Brandyman”), Henry McQuead and John Fulton of Easttown. There were many ways of spellinng the Neely family name. which appear on these pages are an accurate representation of the many variations found in documents of the 18th and 19th centries. For example, it is splet two different ways in th title of a 1795 court petition.

James Davis (1767) and John Dunbar (1768 - 1769) were assessed for a fulling mill, probably the same one, and William Bailey is listed as a fuller (one who bleaches or whitens wool or cloth). 

There were blacksmith shops in the vicinity of the Spread Eagle, Paoli, Howell’s, and the Leopard at a very early date. Later, David, a son of William Evans, the first blacksmith at Paoli, ran a shop in addition to a hundred acre farm. Paul Sharraden (1769 - 1774) and Joel WattsJoshua Evans , Spread Eagle, Thomas Pennington, Howell’s tavern and Morris Davis also followed the blacksmith trade. Joseph Massey, Anthony Thomas, and Thomas Watkins ran the Easttown shops.

Joshua Evans was a carpenter until he turned to tavern keeping and politics at Paoli. Humphrey Wain is listed as a “joyner”; Robert Fullerton, painter; William Pomroy, tinsman; Robert McGuigan (Easttown), butcher; Joshua Humphreys, clockmaker; Peter Mather (later taven keeper at the Warren), vendue cryer; and Benjamin Ronbinson, lemon peddler.

Perhaps there is no business more simple and lucrative than that of distilling spirits. This became clear during the first few years of the Prohibition. In the early history of the country the distillation of strong drink was one of the first industries engaged in as an honorable employment and there were many unrecorded stills for rye whiskey. One was located on the Davis farm just below Howell’s tavern, another at the “Black Swan” in the wooded ravine below Neeley’s and another just back of Neeley’s on the hillside.

The Neeley log cabin still stands on Old State road one block north of T/E Middle School and is used as a residence today.

Swift flowing water is needed to power a mill. Easttown has but a short stretch of the Darby creek of sufficient the emigrant, came from Merionethshire, Wales, 1708, with his wife Jean and son John. Ellis Pugh also came on the same ship and taught young John his ABC's on shipboard. John Morris' grandson, Lewis, came from Hilltown, Bucks County to Easttown in 1764 and bought land, some of which is still in this family.

Sometime during the late colonial or pre-Revolutionary period a straggling hamlet of less than a score of humble homes came to be known as Cockletown. It extended for half a mile or more along the Lancaster, later known as the Conestoga or Old road; from a short distance in Easttown east of the Fox tavern (Francis avenue), to a little beyond Peggy’s corner (Howellville road) in Tredyffrin; and flourished up to the Turnpike era.

Although situated on the first and chief inland highway of the province, it was somewhat isolated locally. The nearest crossroads, the Welsh Line or Baptist road, was a mile to the east and the Bear road a mile and a half to the west.

There then existed, however, a private wood road or right of way, through the Atkinson, later John Reese land, leading down to the valley and on out to the Swedesford road (today’s Circuit City store) near Wilson’s Corner.

Another bypath began at Peggy’s Corner, which gave access to the Neilley’s and continued down the wooded ravine to the Black Swan distillery and beyond through the Reese plantation, with several gates, to the Swedesford road opposite the present entrance to Chesterbrook.

A third ancient lane, a quarter of a mile west of Peggy’s Corner, entered deeply in the hills and turned to a dead end in Prissy’s bottom (where today’s Bodine road turns uphill to the south), giving access to the residents of some five or six log houses on the southern exposure of the hills; but this right of way extended no further, except by footpath, to Howell’s Tavern, now Howellville. 

Scarcely more than a hundred yards north of the Old road at any point and sometimes bordering it, was an almost unbroken forest of deciduous timber, with here and there a stand of pitch pine, and frequently a dense border of red cedar. The hills and ravines of the Slate ridge, or South Valley hills, had also a dense under growth of laurel and wild grape vine; the small bogs or swamps an almost impenetrable mass of spicewood and green-brier.

The dwellings of this early settlement at Cockletown, perhaps the earliest incipient town of Easttown, were mostly of the log cabin type, built of oak or chestnut logs, with stone chimneys; occasionally one more pretentious had stout stone gable ends. However, they were mostly small and homely, erected so close to the right of way that the habitants could step from the doorsill directly into the road. On one side was the wood pile and the well with its windlass and oaken bucket; on the other the lye barrel, the lilac bush, the clump of hollyhocks, and more than likely the pig pen.

Few of these squatters, tenants or small land owners kept a horse; but few were without a cow, at least two hogs, and a flock of poultry.

The cleared plots were not extensive, though ample to grow enough corn, potatoes, cabbage, turnips, and pumpkins to carry the stock and family over the winter. They planted five grains of corn to the hill, according to the proverb:

One for the blackbird one for the crow;
one to rot, and two to grow.

However remote from town, Cockletown was by no means lonely. Until about 1730 the Old road had been almost exclusively a packhorse trail, as it had been more anciently an Indian path. Later it became a thoroughfare fifty feet wide for traders, emigrants, drovers, freighters in Conestoga wagons, etc., deep in mire or dust, according to the season or state of the weather, and the small homesteader could no longer plant his corn in the middle of the road and require the occasional traveler to detour as best he could.

This hamlet, was only locally known at Cockletown., but whether given in honor of the alleged ancient Welsh national flower, the corn cockle, as some say, or in disrespect by the more prosperous farmers, who centrainly regarded the hill clearings as “fit only for growing timber and weeds,” is an open question.

In the Burn family papers there is the statement of Eizabeth Burn, nee Jones, who was born in 1797, four miles east of this place and an actuak resident here from 1832 to 1879. She asserted that this place was called Cockletown and that the name was derived from the cornflower, an imported European weeed closely related to the ragged robin, which flourished and became very troublesome in the wheat fields.

The settlers at first had no other means of lighting their cabins than that furnished by the open fireplace, but after awhile they became more affluent and tallow dips came in fashion.

Well dressed, notched and chinked log dwellings, though snug and warm, had one great fault. The American bug indigenous to the inner bark of the anceient hemlock, frequently transferred to the log cabin and was difficult to eradicate. This condition of affairs gave expression to a none too polite or delicate saying: 

Good night! Sleep tight! Don’t let the bugs bite!

Proceeding westward on the Old Lancaster road in Easttown, there were two small log houses on the north side, one in front of where Westley Jones, shoemaker, built his new frame house in 1862, and the other close to the entrance to the late Dr. Okie’s place. On the south side there was at least one, possibly two, log dwellings.

This land was a small part of the 2000 acre tract patented by William Wood and William Sharlow, surveyed August 21,1684, and in the sub-division of l000 acres of the latter, November 28, 1704. The entire tract then came into the possession of Richard Harrison, and later, September 11, 1746, Samuel Harrison, and 119 acres, later to Standish Ford.,

Then came the Fox tavern, the only building entirely of stone. Its erection is of unknown date. Historian Julius Sachse informs us that it was kept by Fox from 1792 to 1797, and by David Llewellyn until 1804, when it ceased to be a place of public entertainment and became a country store.

Its site marked the extreme northeastern corner of the l000 acre “Travelgwyn” tract of William Wood. The northern quarter section of 250 acres came into the possession of ten persons in succession, the last being Peter Elliot, April 15, 1723.

The old tavern was demolished about 1900 by the late Joseph Williams family to make way for a more modern dwelling. Old English coins have been found while digging in the vicinity, probably relics of the pitch-penny period.

The next tract on the south side of the road is also mostly in Easttown and early belonged to Peter Elliot who was a blacksmith.

The early Tredyffrin ownership of the land on which Cockletown was situated, appears less complicated than that of the Easttown end. William Standly patented 300 acres between the two Welsh lines, Baptist road and the Welsh line near Peggy’s Corner. This was a strip immediately north of the Easttown line. Its entire acreage was acquired by John Day and passed to his widow Hannah (her second husband was James Atkinson) and then to Grace Peadwell, Hannah’s daughter. Thomas Godfrey owned it in 1749. The latter or his son disposed of the aforesaid tract in smaller parcels and all of the western part is included in the ancient hamlet of Cockletown.

On the north side of the Old road there was a stone and log dwelling about where Dr. Wharton’s house stood, but closer to the road. This may have been built by Abel Thomas, carpenter, who owned about 70 acres in the vicinity, mostly in the woods, in 1783. This house was later occupied by Widow Jane Dane after she had retired from the Springhouse Tavern.

A short distance west and on the opposite side of the road there was a blacksmith shop The site was probably immediately in front of the cottage built much later by Levering Latch, where scrap iron and a cannon ball were unearthed. The late Mrs. Benjamin Longaker, nee Lewis, has said that she remembered this building from her early girlhood when it was in a tumbledown condition. It had the appearance even then of being very ancient and was reputed haunted-lights appearing in the windows as if the ghost of the blacksmith had returned and was busied relighting the forge.

The John Reese house, later the residence of the Rev. Dr. Sagebeer, doubtless dates from the Reese ownership. This, of logs, is now weather-boarded. The low, long barn dated from 1830 and was removed about 1880.

Abel Reese in his will, January 8, 1797, bequeathed to his son John, his plantation of 63 acres, he to pay his sisters Judith and Elizabeth, Â£100. The first house on this farm, was a small one of logs close to the public road, on the extreme southwest corner of that position of land north of the Old road and close to the entrance of the wood road to the valley. It was probably built by John Thomas or earlier, in Atkinson’s time. This building was removed about 1876.

The original Drove Tavern (or taverns, since the story goes that there were two connected by an underground passage) was on the site of the later Fritz house, and was reached from the Old Lancaster road by a lane. In 1779 it was said to be kept by Thomas Search; certainly, either this or the last Drove on the Turnpike was kept by John Reese and his son Abel.

On the North side of the Old road and west of the John Reese farm, was the Burns farm, as it became known. Thomas Godfrey parceled out the Standly grant in smaller lots as before mentioned; forty acres to Thomas McKean and thirty acres to John Shaw in 1750. Shaw sold to Enoch James, James transferred the same to Christian Brannaman, usually listed as “Brandy man,” and the executors of the latter to Sebastian Rink. McKean also sold to Rink.

McKean was landlord at the Blue Ball Tavern and was taxed in Easttown for 400 acres of land. He was the largest landowner there in 1765. Heretofore we have had Welsh, Scotch-Irish and English owners, but Brannaman and Rink were Germans. A marker was erected by the D.A.R. over the grave at St. Peter’s of Ensign George King, who is said to have been a younger son of a German baron. He married in 1756, Catherine, daughter of Christian Brannaman.

Rink was a shoemaker. The records show that he did not come in absolute possession of the eastern tract of 30 acres until 1765 and the western tract of 40 acres until 1769, though he was probably in residence earlier. His first assessment was erroneously from Easttown. His residence on the western tract not far from the only available spring would seem to indicate an agreement for its purchase, and it was he who replaced the original log cabin with a mansion (in those days) of thick stone gable walls and dressed log front and rear, and caused to be traced deeply in the wet mortar of a countersunk square high up in the west gable “B.R. 1767”.

In 1775, after the sale to Christopher Rue, Rink disappeared. This was not an uncommon subterfuge, during the Revolution to prevent confiscation should the Crown prevail. Rue, who was a lieutenant of the Easttown militia, conveyed the property to Andrew Steel of the Leopard Tavern, in 1779, two years after Steel, a non-combatant had conveyed it to Joseph Griffith, an officer in the Tredyffrin militia. Both officers filed lists of damages inflicted by the British army, aggregating 67 pounds, 2 shillings and 3 pence. The house was later the residence of George P. Orr, who greatly enlarged and remodeled it.

The next habitation was immediately in front of the Robert Doyle residence, long known as Peggy’s Corner, an ancient log cote which Dr. Quimby immortalized in his novel “Valley Forge” as “Peggy Hambleton’s Cake and Beer Shop.” Old English coins have been excavated here. Later the site was only a heap of stones at the foot of an ancient cedar. It was replaced by the present small house on the southeast corner of Howellville and State roads in 1846.

The last house on the Old road in Cockletown was near the former MacNamee house later occupied by S. Paul Teamer. It was a long, low structure of logs and of two periods: the easternmost section very old; the western end built later where a tenant at one time kept a night school. It was called “Corner Lott” in the 1792 will of old Abel Reese when bequeathed to wife Violetta. This tract was mainly west of the old Welsh line which ran from the Newtown Street road through Easttown. A very early owner was Richard Iddings whose daughter Elizabeth was the mother of General Anthony Wayne.

Not all of the houses of Cockletown lay close to the Old road; several were hidden in the folds of the wooded ravines leading down to the valley. In “Lewis’ Hollow”, then reached by a wood road through the Reese land, there was a tract of ten acres. The original log house was embedded in the southern slope of the hill near the upper spring.

“Neilley’s Hollow” also contained inhabitants. There was a small log cabin on the crest of the hill above the springs (in the midst of Doyle’s North Berwyn nursery). This probably belonged to the Reese family at one time. Tradition states its early tenants operated a small distille1y at the source of Trout Run immediately below, probably the Black Swan.

Of the two or three original Cockletown houses now standing, the Neilley house is the oldest. The homestead of one or more acres is said to have been part of an original grant of 100 acres to Thomas and Cadwalader Jones by right of their mother. James Neilley, according to family history, was born in 1750 in the County Antrim, Ireland, came to America in 1768, and set up a handloom for linen weaving in 1775.

This house was built of stone on the living rock, the rear buried in the side of the hill; the superstructure of logs and the original bowed roof was thatched with rye straw. It had one room in the basement, two on the first floor and an unceiled garret. The shop for weaving was an abandoned stable one and a half stories high, with earthen floor and no provision for heating. It stood immediately in front of the house and was demolished about 1880, and a small one-story annex added to the west side of the cottage, which served for a carpet weaving loom for the last Neilley, also a James. In the renovation of this old house, William Doyle was careful to retain all the outward features, so that while the interior was made comfortable, the exterior presents much of the characteristics of by gone days.

Thus did Cockletown, without plan or forethought, come into existence. It was just a typical community of its time, composed mainly of mechanics and small farmers combined, but an essential part of the rural economy of a growing colony.

Doubtless its inhabitants had front row seats for the series of important military events which took place in the neighborhood beginning in the early autumn of 1777. But with the completion of the Turnpike in 1798, Cockletown became just another backwoods settlement and passed into harmless disuse long before the Reeses erected their sign “Reeseville” opposite the Drove Tavern.
